meta.title: Cenote & Reef Diving in Tulum | Kay Diving — PADI Courses & Guided Dives
meta.description: Guided cenote and reef diving in Tulum, from a first try dive to PADI Open Water and Advanced. Equipment, cenote entrance, transport to the dive sites and snacks included. From ${from}.

hero.lede: Kay Diving is a proudly 100% Mexican company with more than 10 years of experience in the area. We guide cenote and reef dives around Tulum — from a first breath underwater to a PADI certification. Our guides do not just take you down; they tell you the history of the place while you are in it.
hero.alt: A diver silhouetted against the turquoise glow of a Tulum cenote, among bare branches rising through the water

about.h2: Three quarters of our planet are water. Let's go and explore them together.
about.p1: At Kay Diving we are passionate about the Mayan underworld. Our guides will not only take you on a personalised experience, they will teach you about the magical history of this place. We also take pride in our responsibility towards the environment, making conscious decisions about the way we protect this beautiful planet.
about.p2: The Riviera Maya has some of the most beautiful diving sites in the world, and some very good dive centres. What we take special pride in is making the tour yours — so that you feel at home, and the day is built around you rather than around a schedule.
about.question: We send you a few questions before the dive. What you have done before, what you want out of the day, what makes you uneasy. It is the difference between a dive that suits you and a dive that merely happens.
about.plateAlt: A Kay Diving guide carrying a tank down to the water in Tulum
about.plateNote: PERSONALISED · every tour built around you

products.intro: Every price below already includes your equipment, the cenote entrance fees, transport between the dive sites and snacks in between dives. Hotel pickup is the one thing quoted separately — see Getting there.

level.open-water-plus: Open Water · Advanced or Deep for Angelita and El Pit

places.playa-del-carmen: Playa del Carmen · 45 min from Tulum

discover-scuba.name: Discover Scuba
discover-scuba.text: Your first glimpse of the underwater world. Learn the basics of scuba, then go and explore an open-air cenote with crystal clear water, no deeper than seven metres. No certification, no previous experience — just a guide, shallow water and a very good morning. The second dive only runs if the sea is right that day.
discover-scuba.alt: A diver in the shafts of light falling through the roots of a Tulum cenote, above the rocks

reef-cenote.name: Reef & Cenote
reef-cenote.text: One day, both halves of what makes this coast worth diving: the reef off Tankah, then the fresh water of Casa Cenote. Salt and sweet, turtles and stalactites, in a single morning.
reef-cenote.alt: Two divers over the green freshwater of Casa Cenote near Tulum

cenote-diving.name: Cenote Diving
cenote-diving.text: Into some of the most beautiful flooded caverns in the world. You choose the cenotes with us, and which ones are open to you depends on your certification — Angelita and El Pit are the two that pass thirty metres.
cenote-diving.alt: A diver under the surface of a Tulum cenote, light falling through the mangrove roots

advanced-ow.name: Advanced Open Water
advanced-ow.text: The next step: five specialty dives taking you to thirty metres, in Cenote Angelita or Cenote El Pit. Learning materials included.
advanced-ow.alt: A diver giving a thumbs-up in the turquoise water of a Tulum cenote, a column of bubbles rising above

open-water.name: Open Water Course
open-water.tagline: Join the fun, become a certified diver.
open-water.text: The full PADI Open Water licence over five dives, between Casa Cenote and the Tankah reef. No previous experience needed. You leave with a certification that works anywhere in the world.
open-water.alt: A diver swimming towards the camera through roots and shafts of light in a Tulum cenote

snorkel.name: Snorkel tour
snorkel.text: For anyone who wants a little adventure and a lot of calm. Three different cenotes across half a day, finishing at one of the best local taquerías in town. No experience needed, and no tank.
snorkel.alt: A snorkeller seen from above, mask and fins on, in turquoise water

bull-sharks.name: Bull Sharks
bull-sharks.text: Every winter the bull sharks come to the coast off Playa del Carmen, and we drive the forty-five minutes to meet them. Two dives from the boat: the first with the sharks, the second on a shallow reef between eight and twenty metres. Advanced Open Water or equivalent, no exceptions.
bull-sharks.alt: Bull sharks in the blue water off Playa del Carmen, remoras alongside

angelita.name: Cenote Angelita
angelita.note: The hydrogen sulphide cloud, with dead branches rising through it.

el-pit.name: Cenote El Pit
el-pit.note: Light falls the whole way down the shaft and simply stands there.

others.name: The other cenotes
others.note: Chosen with you to match your level and what you want from the day.

cenote-diving.title: Cenote diving in Tulum — prices and requirements | Kay Diving
cenote-diving.description: Guided cenote diving in Tulum: two or three dives, equipment, cenote entrance and transport to the sites included. From $200 USD. Open Water required.
cenote-diving.lede: Two or three dives inside the flooded caverns of the Riviera Maya, with a guide who knows each one. You pick the day's cenotes with us.
cenote-diving.who: This one is for certified divers. With Open Water you dive the cenotes that stay inside eighteen metres, which is most of them and the finest for light. Angelita and El Pit drop past thirty, and those ask for Advanced Open Water or Deep Diver — that is not our rule, it is the depth. If you have never dived, this is not yours yet: start with the Discover Scuba, which exists for exactly that. We dive four divers per guide at most, and the ratio is not negotiable: more people means more guides — a group of eight goes together, with two.
day: We leave at 8:00, 8:30 or 9:00 in the morning. If we pick you up in Tulum town or a little outside it, the transport is added when you book; if you make your own way, we meet at the meeting point.

Before the first dive we fit your gear with you and run the briefing: where the line goes, what you will see, how long it lasts. In a cenote that is not a formality — the orientation is what makes the dive a calm one.
Each dive runs thirty to forty-five minutes. Between them there is a break with snacks, which are included, and the drive to the next cenote if the day takes in two.
Choose three dives and the first two are at Dos Ojos, with the third at another cenote you pick. With two, the whole day is built around whatever you want to see.
cenote-diving.sites: The day's cenotes are chosen with you, and which ones are open to you depends on your certification. Each has its own page with the depth, what it is like inside, and how far it is from Tulum.

faq.q: Do I need a certification to dive cenotes?
faq.a: Yes. This dive asks for Open Water or above. Without a certification you can still dive with us on the Discover Scuba, a guided dive made for a first time.
Four at most. More people means more guides: a group of eight goes together, with two guides. The ratio does not move.
No. It is cavern diving: always within the zone where daylight is visible and the exit is in sight, following the guideline. Cave diving proper is a different certification and a different thing.
Most of the cenotes stay inside eighteen metres. Angelita reaches thirty-eight and El Pit thirty-two, and those ask for Advanced or Deep.
Cenote water sits around twenty-five degrees all year. The wetsuit is included.

faq.q: Can I choose which cenotes we dive?
faq.a: Yes, and it is part of how the day is built. You tell us what you want to see, we tell you what is within your level, and you make the final pick when you book.
Two dives $200 USD per person, three dives $250 USD. Equipment, cenote entrance, transport between sites and snacks are included; hotel pickup is added separately.

open-water.title: PADI Open Water course in Tulum — price and length | Kay Diving
open-water.description: Get certified as a PADI Open Water diver in Tulum: three days, five dives between Casa Cenote and the Tankah reef, materials and licence included. $600 USD.
open-water.h1: PADI Open Water course in Tulum
open-water.lede: The certification that lets you dive anywhere in the world, over three days and five dives, between an open cenote and the reef. No previous experience needed.
open-water.who: For anyone who has never dived, or who has done one try dive and wants the real certification. We ask for no experience: what you do need is to be comfortable in water and able to swim. The course is the same PADI certification taught everywhere in the world, and the card you leave with does not expire.
day: The course runs over three days. Each one starts between eight and nine in the morning and ends between three and four in the afternoon.

The theory can be done two ways, and both lead to exactly the same certification: online before you arrive, in which case the three days here are water only; or spread across those same three days, between one dive and the next. The first leaves you more free time in Tulum; the second spares you studying before your holiday.

The water starts at Casa Cenote, at seven metres. Open, shallow and clear: that is where the skills are practised — clearing a mask, recovering a regulator, controlling buoyancy — until they come without thinking. It is the best classroom there is.
The last day is two dives on the Tankah reef, one at eleven metres and one at eighteen. Those close the course: the same skills, now where they actually matter.
At the end we register you with PADI and the card is issued in your name. The licence is in the price: there is no surprise charge at the finish.
open-water.sites: The course runs between Casa Cenote, an open brackish cenote beside the sea, and the Tankah reef. Two different settings on purpose: what you learn in one you use in the other.

faq.q: How long does the course take?
faq.a: Three days. Each day starts between eight and nine in the morning and ends between three and four in the afternoon.

faq.q: Do I need to know how to dive?
faq.a: No. The course is built for someone starting from nothing. All we ask is that you are comfortable in water and can swim.

faq.q: Do I have to study before I arrive?
faq.a: Whichever you prefer. The theory can be done online beforehand, in which case the three days here are diving only; or during those three days, between one dive and the next. The certification is the same either way.

faq.q: How deep does the course go?
faq.a: The first dives, at Casa Cenote, are at seven metres. The last day is two dives on the Tankah reef, one at eleven metres and one at eighteen, and those close the course.
The five dives, full equipment, the course materials, site entrance, snacks, transport between sites and the PADI licence. $600 USD per person.

faq.q: Is the certification valid in other countries?
faq.a: Yes. Open Water is PADI's entry certification and is recognised at any dive centre in the world. It does not expire.
To eighteen metres, with a certified buddy and without a guide if you want. For Tulum's deep cenotes — Angelita, El Pit — the next step is the Advanced.

discover-scuba.title: Discover Scuba in Tulum — dive without a certification | Kay Diving
discover-scuba.description: Your first dive in Tulum, guided and with no certification, in the clear water of Casa Cenote. It counts as the first dive of the Open Water course. From $140 USD.
discover-scuba.lede: A first time underwater, guided from start to finish, in an open cenote of clear and shallow water. No certification, no experience.
discover-scuba.who: For anyone who has never breathed underwater and wants to know what it feels like before committing to a course. We ask for nothing beforehand beyond being comfortable in water. It is not a certification: it is a guided dive, with an instructor beside you the whole time, and never past seven metres. In the cenotes we dive four divers per guide at most, and the ratio is not negotiable: more people means more guides.
day: On land first, the essentials: how to breathe through the regulator, how to equalise your ears, the few hand signals you will use down there. Short on purpose — what you need to be calm, not an exam.
Then we practise those same things standing up, in the shallow part of Casa Cenote, until they come without thinking.
And then the dive, around forty-five minutes, with the instructor beside you. Casa Cenote is open, clear and shallow: you can see the sky from below and the mangroves reach into the water.
Choose two dives and the second is nothing like the first — you are no longer thinking about breathing, you are looking.
discover-scuba.sites: Casa Cenote, a few minutes from Tulum. An open brackish cenote beside the sea, mangroves along its edges: shallow, clear and calm, which is exactly what a first time needs.

faq.a: No. That is what this dive is for: it is guided from start to finish and asks for nothing beforehand.
To seven metres, the limit for this kind of dive. Casa Cenote is shallow for exactly that reason.
Four at most in the cenotes. More people means more guides.
About forty-five minutes underwater, plus the briefing and practice before it.
One dive $140 USD per person, two dives $200 USD. Gear, cenote entrance, transport to the site and snacks are included.

faq.q: And if I want to certify afterwards?
faq.a: It counts in your favour: this dive is taken as the first of the five on the Open Water course. The next step is three days, and you leave with a certification valid anywhere in the world.

reef-cenote.title: Reef and cenote in one day, in Tulum | Kay Diving
reef-cenote.description: Two dives in a day: the Tankah reef in salt water and Casa Cenote in fresh. Gear, entrance and transfers included. $200 USD. Open Water required.
reef-cenote.h1: Reef and cenote in one day
reef-cenote.lede: The two halves of what makes this coast worth diving, in the same morning: the reef off Tankah and the fresh water of Casa Cenote.
reef-cenote.who: For Open Water divers with one day who would rather not choose between the two. It is also the best way to understand why people come to dive here: within a few kilometres the water, the light, the life and the feeling all change. In the cenotes we dive four divers per guide at most, and the ratio is not negotiable: more people means more guides.
day: We start on the Tankah reef, in salt water. A low, calm reef, the kind you dive without current and with good visibility.
Then the fresh water. Casa Cenote is minutes away: open, with mangroves reaching into the water and light falling between the roots. The difference with an hour ago is total.
Between the two there is a break with snacks, included, and the drive between the sites.
Each dive runs about forty-five minutes and neither goes past nine metres, so the day asks a lot of your eyes and nothing of your lungs.
reef-cenote.sites: The Tankah reef and Casa Cenote, both minutes from Tulum and minutes from each other.

faq.a: Open Water or above. Neither dive goes past nine metres.

faq.q: Why a reef and a cenote on the same day?
faq.a: Because they are two different worlds fifteen minutes apart, and seeing them back to back is what makes this coast make sense.
Four at most in the cenote. More people means more guides.
Both dives, the gear, the cenote entrance, transport between the sites and snacks. $200 USD per person.

faq.q: Is there current on the reef?
faq.a: Tankah is a low, sheltered reef. This is not a current dive or a deep one.

advanced-ow.title: PADI Advanced Open Water course in Tulum — two days | Kay Diving
advanced-ow.description: PADI Advanced Open Water certification in Tulum over two days: five specialty dives to thirty metres, at Angelita or El Pit. Certification included. $550.
advanced-ow.h1: PADI Advanced Open Water course in Tulum
advanced-ow.lede: Five specialty dives across two days, taking you to thirty metres and opening Tulum's two deep cenotes. Materials and certification included.
advanced-ow.who: For divers who already hold the Open Water and want two things: depth, and the cenotes that ask for it. Angelita and El Pit are closed to an Open Water diver — not by a rule of ours, but because they go past thirty metres — and this course is the door. In the cenotes we dive four divers per guide at most, and the ratio is not negotiable: more people means more guides.
day: The Advanced is not theory with an exam at the end: it is five specialty dives, and you learn by doing them. The study materials are included.
Two days is the usual shape: two dives on the first, three on the second. If you would rather not fill the day, it spreads over three — two, two and one. Your call.
Four of the five specialties are fixed: deep diving, underwater navigation, peak performance buoyancy and night diving. The fifth is yours to pick, between drift diving, nitrox and cavern diving.

The deep dives are done at Cenote Angelita or El Pit, the two deep cenotes in the area and among the most striking sites you will ever dive. At Angelita there is a cloud of hydrogen sulphide at around thirty metres, with dead branches rising through it; at El Pit the light comes down the whole shaft and simply stays there.
You finish certified to thirty metres, and those two cenotes stop being closed to you.
advanced-ow.sites: Cenote Angelita and Cenote El Pit, the two deep cenotes near Tulum. Each has its own page with the depth and what it is like inside.

faq.q: How long does the course take?
faq.a: Usually two days: two dives on the first, three on the second. It can also be done over three, with two, two and one. You decide.
Four are fixed: deep diving, underwater navigation, peak performance buoyancy and night diving. The fifth is your pick, between drift diving, nitrox and cavern diving.

faq.q: What do I need to start the course?
faq.a: The Open Water certification, or the equivalent from another agency.
To thirty metres, which is the Advanced limit and what opens Angelita and El Pit.
The deep dives, at Cenote Angelita or El Pit.
Four at most in the cenotes. More people means more guides.
The five specialty dives, the gear, the study materials, cenote entrance, transport, snacks and the Advanced Open Water certification itself. $550 USD per person.

bull-sharks.title: Bull shark diving in Playa del Carmen | Kay Diving
bull-sharks.description: Two boat dives with bull sharks off Playa del Carmen, November to March. We leave from Tulum. $250 USD. Advanced Open Water required.
bull-sharks.lede: Every winter female bull sharks come in to the coast off Playa del Carmen. We drive the forty-five minutes and get in with them.
bull-sharks.who: For divers with Advanced Open Water or the equivalent, no exceptions — this is boat diving, in open water, with large animals. If you hold the Open Water and want to do this, the way there is the Advanced first.
day: We leave Tulum early and drive the forty-five minutes to Playa del Carmen. From there, onto the boat.
The first dive is the shark dive. The second is on a low reef, between eight and twenty metres.

These are wild animals, free: they come because the season brings them, not because anyone calls them. That is exactly what makes it worth doing, and also what means nobody can promise you how many you will see.
The season runs November to March. Outside those months they are not there, and we do not sell it.
bull-sharks.sites: Off Playa del Carmen, forty-five minutes from Tulum, from a boat.

faq.a: November to March. Outside those months the bull sharks are not on the coast and we do not run the trip.
Advanced Open Water or the equivalent, no exceptions.
It cannot be guaranteed. These are wild animals in open water; the season is very reliable, but a sighting is never a promise.
No. It is open-water diving from a boat, with a guide.
Both dives, the gear, transport from Tulum and snacks. $250 USD per person.

snorkel.title: Cenote snorkelling tour in Tulum | Kay Diving
snorkel.description: Half a day snorkelling three cenotes near Tulum, no certification and no experience needed. Gear, entrance and transport included. $125 USD per person.
snorkel.lede: Three different cenotes in half a day, no tank, no course and no rush. We finish at one of the best taquerías in town.
snorkel.who: For anyone who wants to see the cenotes from the inside without taking up diving: families, someone along with a diver, or anyone who would rather stay at the surface. No experience and no certification, and the snorkelling gear is included. There is no minimum age.
day: Half a day, three cenotes. Each one different from the last on purpose: the shape, the light and what you see from above all change.
From the surface you see more than people expect. In clear, shallow water with light coming down from above, the bottom and the formations are there in full.
Between one and the next there is the drive and snacks, included, and the pace is whatever the group's is.
And at the end, tacos. Not part of the price — part of the day.
snorkel.sites: Three of our favourite cenotes near Tulum, chosen on the day according to the water and what the group wants to see.

faq.q: Do I need to know how to dive?
faq.a: No. This is snorkelling: you breathe at the surface, with a mask and snorkel. No certification of any kind.
Mask and snorkel, entrance to all three cenotes, transport between them and snacks. $125 USD per person.
It starts between eight and nine in the morning and ends between one and two in the afternoon. Half a day, unhurried.
No. Tell us the ages when you book and we build the day around the group.

faq.q: Is it alright for a weak swimmer?
faq.a: Tell us before you book and we build the day around it. There are vests, and the cenotes are chosen on the day.
Swimwear, a towel and biodegradable sunscreen. We bring the rest.

included.h2:
What you are not
paying extra for.
included.intro: Dive centres in Tulum quote in very different ways. Here is exactly what our prices already cover — and the one thing that is charged separately.

equipment.name: Equipment
equipment.text: High quality gear, fitted before you get in. Snorkel and mask are provided on snorkel tours. Bring a swimsuit and reef-safe sunscreen.

entrance.name: Cenote entrance
entrance.text: The entry fee to every cenote on your day is in the price. No cash gate to pay at the door.

snacks.name: Snacks & water
snacks.text: Food and water between dives. Cenote mornings run longer than people expect.

site-transport.name: Transport to the sites
site-transport.text: From the meeting point to every cenote and back, all day. Hotel pickup is separate — see below.

materials.name: Learning materials
materials.text: On both courses, everything you need to study is included.

padi-licence.name: PADI licence
padi-licence.text: Both courses end with a certification recognised worldwide, included in the price.

gallery.h2:
What it actually
looks like down there.

captions.gallery-bull-shark: A bull shark off Playa del Carmen

reviews.h2: What divers say once they are back on dry land.
reviews.intro: Five of the reviews Kay Diving has on Google, word for word, in the language each diver wrote them in.

visit.intro: Worth seeing even on a day you are not diving. Where Kay dives is in the cenote guide.
visit.note: Hours, prices and rules change without notice, and every cenote is run by someone different: check on the day before you set off. Cavern diving needs specific training, equipment and a guide — it is not something to improvise.

gran-cenote.name: Gran Cenote
gran-cenote.blurb: One of the best known near Tulum. Boardwalks, clear water, fish and limestone formations in plain sight. A good first cenote, with nothing complicated about it.
gran-cenote.tip: Arrive early — it fills up in high season. Water shoes, and check the sunscreen rules on the day.

dos-ojos.name: Cenote Dos Ojos
dos-ojos.blurb: Two pools linked like a pair of eyes, water you can see straight through, and shafts of light crossing the cavern. One of the emblematic karst sites, above the surface and below it.
dos-ojos.tip: Cavern diving is not recreational diving: it takes specific training. Book through an authorised operator.

tak-be-ha.name: Taak Bi Ha
tak-be-ha.blurb: An enclosed cavern of stalactites over water that barely looks like water. More intimate than the open cenotes, and spectacular when light finds its way in.
tak-be-ha.tip: The formations break at a touch. Keep your hands to yourself and follow the guide.

casa-cenote.name: Casa Cenote (Manatí)
casa-cenote.blurb: A long blue-green channel winding through mangrove, more river than well. Fresh water and salt water meeting a step from the coast.
casa-cenote.tip: Leave the mangrove roots alone and do not feed anything. The halocline shows best when the water is still.

calavera.name: Cenote Calavera
calavera.blurb: Round openings in the rock roof that read as a skull from directly above. Very photogenic, entered by ladder or by jumping.
calavera.tip: Do not jump without checking the depth and without the staff saying yes.

car-wash.name: Cenote Car Wash (Aktun Ha)
car-wash.blurb: A wide pool ringed with greenery, more open and better lit than the caverns. Visibility shifts with the weather and with what the previous days brought.
car-wash.good: Swimming, snorkelling, diving with an operator
car-wash.tip: Check the day's conditions: not every part of it suits every level.

zacil-ha.name: Cenote Zacil-Ha
zacil-ha.blurb: An open cenote with facilities to stay a few hours. The comfortable option when you are a group, or travelling with children.
zacil-ha.tip: Check hours and prices before setting off — they move with the season.

cristal-escondido.name: Cenotes Cristal and Escondido
cristal-escondido.blurb: Two open-air pools in the forest, visited on the same trip. Enough to compare two waterscapes without giving the whole day to one.
cristal-escondido.tip: Bring drinking water and sun cover — there is not much shade.

corazon-paraiso.name: Cenote Corazón del Paraíso
corazon-paraiso.blurb: A pool shaped like a heart from the right angle, surrounded by green. Less roadside than the cenotes on the main route.
corazon-paraiso.tip: Check the access is open before you go, and use nothing that would foul the water.

tankah.name: Tankah cenotes
tankah.blurb: A coastal stretch where cenotes, forest and sea run into each other. What you get depends on which cenote and which operator.
tankah.tip: Ask which cenote exactly, and what is included: transport, guide, equipment or food.

ruins.intro: What is nearby, how long it takes to get there, and how long to give it. For the days you are not in the water.
ruins.priceNote: INAH reference prices, checked {date}. At several sites the ticket is not the whole bill: CULTUR, park or parking fees can be added on top. Confirm before you go.
ruins.ferryNote: Bus to Playa del Carmen, ferry to Cozumel, then local transport. Check the return times before you leave.

tulum.name: Tulum archaeological site
tulum.blurb: A walled Maya city on a cliff above the Caribbean. The most recognisable image on this coast, and the busiest.
tulum.see: El Castillo and the walled precinct; the sea views from the marked lookouts.
tulum.combine: Parque del Jaguar, the Museo de la Costa Oriental, a cenote on the way back.

coba.name: Cobá
coba.blurb: A large Maya city deep in forest, joined by the raised roads called sacbeob. Wider and greener than Tulum, and more walking.
coba.see: The open archaeological groups and the ancient causeways. Ask on site which structures are accessible.
coba.combine: The Choo-Ha, Tankach-Ha and Multum-Ha cenotes.

muyil.name: Muyil
muyil.blurb: A small settlement wrapped in vegetation on the edge of the Sian Ka'an reserve. Quiet, exactly where the others are full.
muyil.see: The structures and the marked trails. The lagoon trip is booked separately, through an authorised operator.
muyil.combine: The Muyil lagoon and Sian Ka'an by boat.

xelha.name: Xelhá archaeological site
xelha.blurb: Maya remains on the coastal corridor, compact and quickly seen. Not the Xel-Há water park, however similar the name and however close they sit.
xelha.see: The structures inside the precinct, on a short circuit.
xelha.combine: The Xel-Há park, on a separate ticket, only if you fancy it.

xcaret.name: Xcaret archaeological site
xcaret.blurb: A coastal Maya settlement inside the Xcaret grounds. The archaeological ticket and the park ticket are two different things — one does not include the other.
xcaret.see: The accessible remains and their setting by the sea.
xcaret.combine: The Xcaret park, if you buy its own entry.

ek-balam.name: Ek' Balam
ek-balam.blurb: Monumental architecture and exceptional carved reliefs, ringed by forest in Yucatán. Far, but unlike anything else on this list.
ek-balam.see: The Acropolis and the open structures. Access to the stairways changes with conservation and safety.

chichen-itza.name: Chichén Itzá
chichen-itza.blurb: One of the great centres of the Maya world, and a World Heritage site. Monumental, heavily visited, and a full day from Tulum.
chichen-itza.see: El Castillo, the Great Ball Court and the Temple of the Warriors, from the permitted areas.
chichen-itza.combine: A cenote nearby and Valladolid, if the timetable allows.

san-gervasio.name: San Gervasio (Cozumel)
san-gervasio.blurb: A ceremonial centre tied to the cult of Ixchel, in the forest of Cozumel. It needs a ferry, so plan it as a full day on the island.
san-gervasio.see: The plazas, the structures and the paths between them.
san-gervasio.combine: San Miguel de Cozumel, beaches and snorkelling.

quote.text: Your safety comes first — and once it is taken care of, all that is left is to enjoy every minute underwater.

book.intro: A deposit holds the date. We confirm by WhatsApp within a few hours, send you a few questions, and you settle the balance on the day.

items.q: Do I need to be certified to dive here?
items.a: Not to start. Discover Scuba takes people who have never breathed underwater, and the snorkel tour needs nothing at all. Every dive to 20 metres or shallower — the reef and most cenotes — needs Open Water or an equivalent. Anything deeper — Angelita and El Pit — needs at least Advanced Open Water or an equivalent; a Deep speciality counts. Bring the card or a digital copy and show it to your guide on the day: without it, we cannot take you on the dive.

items.q: How deep do the dives go?
items.a: Discover Scuba stays at seven metres (25 ft). The Open Water course and the reef stay around nine metres. Most cenote dives are planned to eighteen metres. The two deep ones go further: Cenote Angelita reaches 35–38 metres and Cenote El Pit 30–32. The Advanced course works to 27 metres (90 ft).

items.q: What is actually included in the price?
items.a: High quality equipment, the cenote entrance fees, transport from the meeting point to every site and back, and snacks and water. Both courses also include the learning materials. Hotel pickup is the one thing charged separately — see below. Prices are quoted in dollars and pesos; if you settle the balance in dollars, the exchange rate of the day applies.

items.q: Can you pick me up from my hotel?
items.a: We meet at Easy Chango Dive Center in Tulum at no extra cost. If you are staying in Tulum town we can collect you and drop you back for $20 for the whole booking. If you are outside town or in the hotel zone we cannot collect you, but we can drive you back afterwards for $10.

Three departures: 08:00–13:00, 08:30–13:30 and 09:00–14:00. You can suggest another time when you book — we check it and confirm. Two cenote dives have to start by 13:30 at the latest, and a single dive at Casa Cenote can start as late as 15:00.

items.q: What is the difference between cavern and cave diving?
items.a: Cavern diving stays inside the natural daylight zone, within reach of the entrance and always with a direct route to the surface. Cave diving goes beyond daylight and needs its own certification — a different qualification entirely, and not something an Open Water card covers.
Cenotes sit at roughly 24–25 °C every day of the year, and the reef is a little warmer. Wetsuits are part of the equipment we provide — tell us if you run cold.

Fresh rainwater floating on heavier salt water. The boundary between them refracts light, so swimming through it looks like the water has turned to oil or frosted glass — then it closes behind you and the view snaps back. It is one of the strangest things you will see underwater.

items.q: Why do you send questions before the dive?
items.a: Because a tour built around you is better than a tour built around a schedule. We want to know what you have done before, what you are hoping for, and what makes you uneasy — so the day fits, rather than merely happening.

items.q: When is the best time of year to come?
items.a: Cenotes are sheltered from wind and swell, so they dive well all year. Light beams in the cenotes are strongest around the middle of the day. Reef conditions are generally best in the spring and early summer.

items.casa-cenote: An open, lagoon-like cenote connected directly to the Caribbean Sea, where fresh and salt water mix into an ecosystem of its own. It is about 9 metres deep at most — ideal for new divers and for anyone after a relaxed dive. Mangroves surround it, and the visibility, though it varies, puts you alongside fish, turtles and now and then a freshwater crocodile (Morelet's crocodile, Crocodylus moreletii). The perfect way to combine recreational diving with wildlife up close.
items.car-wash: Under a calm, easy-to-reach surface hides one of the most photographed cenotes on the Riviera Maya. Water lilies float on its clear water; further down there are petrified trunks and a striking gallery of stalactites and stalagmites. Up to 16 metres deep, it suits snorkelling as well as cavern diving, and the sunbeams filtering through the trees turn every dive into something almost cinematic.
items.dos-ojos: One of the most famous flooded cave systems in the world: two connected cenotes that, seen from above, look like a pair of eyes. Its cavern routes, such as “The Barbie Line” and “The Bat Cave”, run through crystal-clear water with more than 30 metres of visibility, past striking stalactites and ancient rock formations. The open areas are about 10 metres deep at most. It belongs to the longest underwater cave system in the world, some 369 kilometres of it. An excellent choice if you have never dived a cenote before.
items.el-pit: One of the deepest and most dramatic cenotes on the Riviera Maya, going down to 119 metres. It is famous for the column of light that pierces the water, for its halocline — where fresh and salt water meet — and for a cloud of hydrogen sulphide at about 30 metres that looks like fog underwater. Recommended for advanced or technical divers, it is one of the most striking cenote dives in the world.
items.angelita: About 60 metres deep, this cenote holds one of the most striking sights in cavern diving: a cloud of hydrogen sulphide lying on the salt water at around 30 metres, which creates the illusion of an underground river, with trunks and fallen leaves “floating” in mid-air. Passing through it feels like crossing a threshold into another dimension, onto a sunken landscape wrapped in a ghostly haze. A mystical, overwhelming experience, reserved for advanced divers looking for something truly unique.
items.dreamgate: A cavern cenote with a round entrance, known for its extraordinarily clear water and for the imposing columns and rock formations that reach down to the bottom. Natural light filtering through the opening above creates spectacular effects. Ideal for cavern diving, with routes through wide chambers and an almost ceremonial atmosphere.
items.tak-be-luum: Less known, and so less touched, this cenote lies in the Dos Ojos park area. It offers cavern passages with well-preserved formations, calm water and a more intimate dive, since it sees fewer visitors. Ideal if you want to explore cenotes off the busiest routes.
items.tak-be-ha: A cave system with wide chambers, sharply defined stalactites and stalagmites, and a strong halocline that blurs the view where fresh and salt water mix. Calm and never crowded, it is ideal for certified divers looking for spectacular formations.
items.nicte-ha: Close to Dos Ojos, it stands out for its aquatic plants and its emerald water, coloured by water lilies and underwater vegetation. Shallower than the other cenotes around it, it is ideal for snorkelling and easy dives, with good visibility and a very photogenic, natural setting.
items.nohoch-nah-chich: Part of one of the longest underwater cave systems in the world. It is known for an astonishing concentration of stalactites and stalagmites, many of them huge, forming real stone “forests” underwater. Its crystal-clear water and intricate passages make it a must for experienced cavern divers looking for formations on another level.
